title: MLPC 02 - Bayesian Decision Theory
subject: Machine Learning and Pattern Classification
description: Covers probabilities and densities, Bayes' rule, posterior classification, conditional risk, MAP decisions, likelihood ratios, and Gaussian decision boundaries. All questions are single-choice and modeled after the conceptual style of the MLPC Retry 2024S exam. Source: 02_Bayesian_Decision_Theory.pdf.

questions.question: A continuous probability density has p(x) = 1.4 at a particular point. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: The density is invalid because it exceeds 1
The event X = x has probability 1.4
This can be valid if the total area under the density is 1
The cumulative probability must be negative

questions.explanation: A density value is not itself a probability and may exceed 1; its integral over the domain must equal 1.

questions.question: For a continuous variable with density p(x), how is P(a <= X <= b) obtained?

options.text: By integrating p(x) from a to b
By counting the number of possible real values

questions.explanation: Probabilities for continuous variables are areas under the density over intervals.

questions.question: In a multivariate Gaussian, what does an off-diagonal covariance entry describe?

options.text: The prior probability of a class
The dimensionality of the output label

questions.explanation: Off-diagonal covariance terms capture how pairs of variables vary together.

questions.question: In Bayes' rule for classification, what does P(omega_i) represent?

options.text: The prior probability of class omega_i
The density of x in every class

questions.explanation: The prior describes class frequency before the current feature observation is considered.

questions.question: In Bayes' rule, what is p(x | omega_i)?

options.text: The probability that class omega_i is correct after observing x
The class-conditional density of observing x within class omega_i
The marginal density of x over all classes
The cost of assigning x to omega_i

questions.explanation: The class-conditional density describes how plausible the observed features are under a given class.

questions.question: What is the role of p(x) in the posterior formula P(omega_i | x) = p(x | omega_i)P(omega_i)/p(x)?

options.text: It normalizes the posteriors so they sum to one
It changes the feature vector into a scalar
It is the prior of omega_i

questions.explanation: The evidence p(x) is shared across classes and normalizes the posterior distribution.

questions.question: Two classes have equal priors. Which class does a MAP classifier choose for observation x?

options.text: The class with the larger p(x | omega_i)
The class with the smaller p(x | omega_i)
The class with the larger loss

questions.explanation: With equal priors, maximizing the posterior is equivalent to maximizing the class-conditional density.

questions.question: A prior assigns probability 1 to class A and 0 to every other class. Assuming that prior is used exactly, what can MAP predict?
questions.explanation: Multiplication by a zero prior gives zero posterior support to every other class.

questions.question: For two classes, P(A | x) = 0.75 and P(B | x) = 0.25. Under zero-one loss, what is the conditional probability of error when predicting A?
questions.explanation: If A is predicted, the error probability is the posterior probability that B is the true class.

questions.question: What does conditional risk R(alpha_i | x) compute?

options.text: The expected loss of action alpha_i, weighted by posterior class probabilities
The density integrated over all feature values

questions.explanation: Conditional risk averages the action's class-dependent losses using the posterior probabilities.

questions.question: What does the general Bayes decision rule choose?

options.text: The action with minimum conditional risk
The class with minimum likelihood in every case

questions.explanation: Bayes-optimal action selection minimizes expected loss for the observed x.

questions.question: Why can a rejection action be useful in Bayesian decision theory?

options.text: It permits an 'I do not know' decision when classification risk is high
It guarantees that all observations receive a class
It changes continuous features into discrete features

questions.explanation: The action set may include rejection when committing to a class would be too costly or uncertain.

questions.question: Under zero-one loss, minimizing conditional risk is equivalent to:
questions.explanation: With zero cost for correct decisions and unit cost for errors, risk is 1 minus the selected class posterior.

questions.question: In a two-class Bayesian classifier, the likelihood ratio is compared with a threshold determined by:
questions.explanation: The input-dependent likelihood ratio is compared with a constant based on prior odds and cost ratios.

questions.question: The cost of predicting omega_1 when omega_2 is true is increased. What generally happens to the decision region for omega_1?

options.text: It must become the entire feature space
It is unaffected by all costs
It becomes identical to the density p(x)

questions.explanation: A higher penalty requires stronger evidence before choosing omega_1, shrinking its decision region.

questions.question: Two Gaussian classes have identical spherical covariance matrices. What form does their Bayes decision boundary have?

options.text: A linear hyperplane perpendicular to the line between their means

questions.explanation: Equal spherical covariances yield a linear separator orthogonal to the line connecting the means.

questions.question: Two Gaussian classes have equal but non-spherical covariance matrices. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Their boundary remains linear but need not be perpendicular to the line between the means

questions.explanation: A shared covariance cancels quadratic terms, leaving a linear boundary whose orientation reflects the covariance.

questions.question: What form can arise when Gaussian classes have different covariance matrices?

options.text: Only a boundary halfway between the means

questions.explanation: Unequal covariance matrices generally leave quadratic terms in the discriminant functions.
